summary: Describes security threats to the Reliable Server Pooling architecture and sets out requirements for security to counter them. RSerPool manages and provides access to pools of servers for highly reliable applications. It is informational.

eli5.summary: Before locking a building you list the ways a burglar could get in. This lists the ways attackers could trouble a group of backup servers, and what protections are needed.

subtitle: Security threats in server pooling and how to counter them.

tldr.problem: When servers form a pool with a distributed registry and clients connect dynamically, attackers can spoof servers, inject false pool data, intercept connections, or overwhelm the registry with floods of requests.
tldr.mechanism: The document catalogs 17 categories of threat and specifies security requirements: mutual authentication using TLS with pre-shared keys, integrity checking, data confidentiality, and rate limiting on critical messages.
tldr.outcome: Security requirements guide the implementation of ASAP and ENRP protocols (defined in companion RFCs) to protect against spoofing, man-in-the-middle attacks, denial of service, and data eavesdropping.

facts.label: Primary security mechanism
facts.value: TLS with pre-shared keys (mandatory to implement)

facts.label: Deployment assumption
facts.value: Single administrative domain controls key distribution

today: RFC 5355 is informational and sets security requirements for RSerPool. As RSerPool itself remained experimental, these security specifications served as a reference for implementations of the ASAP and ENRP protocols. The document remains valid as a threat model for distributed server pooling architectures.

sections.title: Threats to RSerPool
sections.content:
RSerPool provides failover and load balancing by redirecting clients to different servers dynamically. This session-layer transparency exposes new security concerns. The architecture assumes a single administrative domain controlling the pool, but must still defend against unauthorized entities and insider threats.

This RFC catalogs threats specific to RSerPool: attacks on server registration, malicious ENRP servers, spoofing, replay attacks, flooding, and state attacks during failover. For each threat it specifies what security mechanism is required. TLS with pre-shared keys is the chosen mechanism for authenticating peers and protecting data.
sections.eli5: Backup servers are great, but only if you know that the server you get is real, not impersonated. This document lists all the tricks an attacker could try and what you need to do to stop them.

sections.title: Key Security Requirements
sections.content:
Several requirements appear across multiple threats:

Authentication: ENRP servers must authenticate pool elements (PEs) before accepting registration. Similarly, PEs must authenticate ENRP servers before trusting them. ENRP servers must authenticate each other. This prevents unauthorized servers from joining the pool and prevents clients from using rogue ENRP servers. TLS with pre-shared keys (PSK) is mandatory: a network administrator distributes shared keys to legitimate peers.

Integrity: Data in transit between PEs and ENRP servers, and between ENRP servers, must have integrity protection so corruption (accidental or malicious) is detected. TLS provides this.

Confidentiality: Network topology and pool membership information should not be visible to eavesdroppers. TLS encryption protects against this, especially important for inter-provider (multi-SP) scenarios where different organizations operate pools.

Replay Prevention: An attacker must not be able to replay old registration messages to create false state. TLS sequence numbering prevents replay attacks.
sections.eli5: You need three protections: prove who you are, make sure messages are not tampered with, and hide your communication from eavesdroppers. TLS does all three.

sections.title: Categories of Threat
sections.content:
Registration and spoofing attacks: Attackers can flood ENRP servers with fake registrations for non-existent servers, or send false registrations claiming to be legitimate servers. This corrupts the pool database or misdirects clients. Requirement: authenticate PEs before accepting registration.

Malicious ENRP servers: A rogue ENRP server that enters the ENRP peer network can return false server lists to clients or propagate corruption to other ENRP servers. Requirement: ENRP servers must mutually authenticate each other and clients must authenticate ENRP servers.

Handlespace resolution attacks: An attacker posing as an ENRP server can return false addresses in response to pool handle resolution requests, routing clients to a rogue server. Requirement: clients should authenticate ENRP servers using certificates.

Replay attacks: An old registration message could be resent to create false state. Requirement: TLS prevents this with sequence numbers.

Failover security: When a client fails over from one server to another, it may lose the security context (encryption, authentication) established with the first server. Requirement: notify the application of failover so it can re-establish security with the new server.
sections.eli5: Threats come in two flavors: fake servers joining the pool, and fake registries fooling clients. Flooding can lock up the registry. Old messages can be replayed. When switching servers, security settings might be lost.

sections.title: Specific Attack Scenarios
sections.content:
Unauthorized registration flooding: A malicious node sends many false registrations claiming to be legitimate servers. This floods the database and prevents legitimate registrations. TLS with PSK prevents this: only nodes with the correct key can send registrations.

ENRP server discovery spoofing: When a PE tries to discover ENRP servers via multicast, an attacker responds with a spoofed server announcement. The PE might register with the fake ENRP server. Requirement: ENRP servers must authenticate to PEs.

Endpoint-unreachable flooding: A client (PU) could send a flood of Endpoint Unreachable messages to an ENRP server claiming many servers are down. This prevents the ENRP from servicing legitimate requests. Requirement: rate limit these messages.

Keep-Alive flooding: A malicious ENRP server could flood a PE with keep-alive messages during home server takeover, preventing the PE from serving clients. Requirement: ENRP must rate-limit keep-alive frequency.

Cookie mechanism attacks: A PE sends a state cookie to a PU for failover use. If the cookie is not signed, an attacker could forge cookies. Requirement: PEs must sign cookies and other PEs must verify signatures.
sections.eli5: Some attacks waste the registry's time with fake messages. Some fake a registry to fool servers or clients. Others send floods of keep-alive messages. State information must be signed so it cannot be forged.

sections.title: Single Administrative Domain Assumption
sections.content:
RSerPool is designed for deployment within a single administrative domain (one organization, one Service Provider). This assumption simplifies security: the administrator can distribute pre-shared keys to all legitimate nodes. There is no need for a public key infrastructure (PKI) or complex certificate validation.

When RSerPool is used across multiple administrative domains (inter-provider scenarios), additional considerations apply. Topology information must be kept confidential, and policy enforcement becomes more complex. The requirements in this RFC still apply, but implementation details may need adaptation.

This document does not address distributed transactions, data consistency across failover, or authorization granularity beyond the basic authentication requirement. Those are application-level concerns.
sections.eli5: If everyone in the pool is in the same company, the company can simply give everyone a shared password. If pools span different companies, you need stronger guarantees and might hide network details.

left.title: Without authentication
left.desc: Anyone can register a fake server with any pool handle.

right.title: With TLS+PSK
right.desc: Only entities with the correct key can register servers.
